To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
only a third of CCC plans address liver cancer, and of those that do, most do not discuss specific actions needed in their plans to reduce the burden.
27% of comprehensive cancer control plans addressed liver cancer using key search terms and 23 plans addressed HBV and HCV infections as risk factors.

27% of CCC programs in the United States, tribal governments and jurisdictions, and territories and Pacific Island jurisdictions identified at least one goal or objective to reduce liver cancer burden in their plans, but most of these programs did not include specific actions to reduce the burden.

the content of cancer control plans that address chronic hepatitis B or C virus infections as major risk factors for liver cancers.
identifying and analyzing the content of comprehensive cancer control plans in the United States and U.S. territories.
the extent to which chronic hepatitis B and C are addressed as major risk factors for liver cancers and the extent to which CCC programs recommend interventions for liver cancers.

CCC plans in the United States are not currently addressing chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis B virus infections as major risk factors for liver cancers.
CCC programs are addressing chronic viral hepatitis infections as a risk factor for liver cancer and/or recommending interventions for liver cancer in their CCC plans to some extent.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CCC plans in the United States are not consistently addressing HBV and HCV as major risk factors for liver cancers.
there is a need for CCC plans to address HBV and HCV infections as risk factors of primary liver cancer.
the majority of CCC plans do not address HBV and HCV infections as major risk factors for liver cancers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

there is a need for more comprehensive discussion of chronic viral hepatitis in CCC plans and more specific recommendations for reducing the burden of liver and other cancers caused by chronic viral hepatitis.
CCC plans do not adequately discuss HBV and/or hepatitis C infection as risk factors for primary liver cancer or recommend strategies to address this risk factor.

CCC plans should include specific actions to reduce the burden associated with liver cancer, which can be achieved by including specific goals, objectives, and strategies to address chronic hepatitis B or hepatitis C virus infection as a major risk factor for liver cancer.
